name: Rhinoplasty simulation apps

lead: Rhinoplasty simulation software lets a person or a surgeon alter a photo or 3D scan of a nose to show a proposed change. The payoff is seeing a preview of the result immediately and having a clearer plan for nose surgery.

Surgical references describe 3D simulations and 3D cameras that capture and analyse the nose, allow modifications, and help surgeon and patient understand the anatomy. Consumer apps that morph a photo exist alongside clinical systems. The topic appears in looksmaxxing discussion as a way to preview a result before surgery.

paras: Software maps the nose from standard photographs or 3D camera captures and lets the operator reshape contours digitally. Clinics use it in consultations so patient and surgeon can align expectations, and consumer apps offer similar photo morphing.

The tools themselves are low-risk. The surgical result can differ from a simulation because healing, swelling and tissue behaviour vary between individuals; swelling after rhinoplasty can take a year or more to fully settle.

Crisalix: how to communicate surgical outcome clearly

angle.text: Clinics and prospective patients use morphing and 3D imaging software to preview how a nose might look after surgery and to align expectations with the surgeon. The preview image is visible immediately. The actual surgical outcome can differ from it.

lead: Rhinoplasty simulation apps and software let people preview how a nose might look after surgery by editing a photo or a 3D model of their own face. The aim is to see a proposed profile, tip or bridge before committing, and to give surgeon and patient a shared picture of the target [1].

In clinics, the preview is usually built from three photographs taken from different angles, merged into a 3D image, or from a 3D camera capture, and the surgeon then reshapes the nose on screen [1]. Cloud platforms such as Crisalix generate 3D previews from 2D photos or scans and can show treatment options side by side [2]. Consumer apps offer simpler photo morphing.

Published studies have looked at how patients and surgeons perceive these tools and at how closely simulations match results. In a Japanese clinic series, similarity between the simulation and the result correlated with postoperative satisfaction, and a 172-patient series found that most patients felt 3D added value over 2D previews [1][3].
infobox: Several photographs or a 3D camera capture [1][2]
About 10-15 minutes in one clinic series [1]

paras: Rhinoplasty references describe software-based 3D simulation as a way to show existing deformities and plan the proposed approach, and 3D cameras as a way to inspect and edit the nose virtually so that both parties can discuss a likely outcome. Pre-operative consultation also includes a history, an exam of skin type, symmetry, valves and septum, and photographs from several angles, which supply the images these tools work from.

In a Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery Global Open series, a handheld Vectra H1 system took three photographs from different angles and merged them into a 3D image, and a morphed image reflecting the patient's anatomy and aesthetic ideals was produced in roughly 10 to 15 minutes [1]. Crisalix describes a web platform that uses artificial intelligence and cloud technology to create 3D previews from 2D photos or scans and to compare options side by side, with remote viewing for patients [2]. One clinic's description of the Vectra face sculptor says viewers can zoom, rotate the model and compare scenarios such as a nose with and without a chin implant [4].

Healing differs between people and swelling can take at least a year to fully diminish, which affects how closely a preview resembles a final result. Wikipedia reports revision surgery in roughly 5 to 20 percent of rhinoplasties.

Computer-assisted surgical simulation more broadly uses specialised software to render a patient's data as a virtual 3D model and simulate the intervention beforehand, with maxillofacial examples such as navigation in orthognathic surgery [5].

A retrospective single-centre study in Japan of 38 aesthetic rhinoplasty patients who viewed Crisalix 3D simulations used the FACE-Q rhinoplasty module. Similarity between the simulation and the result correlated with satisfaction with the nose (rho 0.66), while surgeon aesthetic scores correlated somewhat more strongly (rho 0.71). The simulation overestimated nasal tip projection by about 0.7 mm and underestimated the nasofrontal angle by about 1.7 degrees; length, alar width and nasolabial angle did not differ significantly. Satisfaction rose from 39.0 to 74.8 after surgery. The authors note the small, retrospective design, follow-up of at least six months, an all-Asian sample, and that simulations do not guarantee results [3].

A 2019 series of 172 rhinoplasty patients compared 2D simulation with 3D morphing. 95 percent of patients said 3D added value over 2D, surgeons saw added value in 66 to 74 percent of patients, and revision patients reported better understanding of the surgical aims (84 percent) than primary patients (61 percent). The study measured perceptions and did not compare simulations with postoperative results [1].

timeline.event: A 172-patient series reports patient and surgeon views of Vectra 3D morphing versus 2D simulation in rhinoplasty consultation [1].
A Japanese series links Crisalix simulation accuracy to FACE-Q satisfaction after rhinoplasty [3].
